q:
The recipe's first printing called for a 'moderate oven,' a phrase that meant something precise to cooks who banked coal fires and meaningless to their grandchildren, who set dials. When the book was reissued, the editor rendered such phrases into degrees — and, some readers complained, edited a small piece of the past out of the book.

It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
options: the grandchildren could not cook at all
'moderate oven' once carried information that a dial setting only partly replaces
coal fires were more accurate than dials
hints: What did the old phrase hold that the new one may not?
It belonged to a whole practice of judging heat by hand and fire.
The complaint suggests something was lost in translation.
expl: The old phrase was precise within its own practice, and readers felt the conversion lost something — so the term carried information a number only partly replaces.

q:
The two candidates for the scholarship had nearly identical grades. What separated them, the committee chair said afterward, was the essay: one listed achievements, while the other showed, through a single summer's work, how a failing community garden was brought back — and what the writer learned when the first plantings died.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Grades are unimportant in scholarship decisions.
When records are equal, a vivid account of real work — including its failures — can be what distinguishes a candidate.
hints: Start from what the chair says actually separated them.
The essays differed in kind: a list versus a story of work and failure.
The main idea must be about that difference, not about grades alone.
expl: With grades equal, the committee was swayed by the essay that showed real work and honest failure over a bare list — choice B states exactly that.

q:
(Transcript) Student: 'I turned in the form for the science fair on Tuesday — sorry, on Thursday — the day the office reopened after the storm.'

According to the student, the form was turned in on
options: the day before the office reopened
hints: The speaker corrects herself mid-sentence.
The correction replaces Tuesday with Thursday.
A self-correction means the second version is the claim.
expl: The student corrects 'Tuesday' to 'Thursday' — in these items the corrected version is the answer, and the office detail confirms the day.

q:
When seeds of the same tomato variety were planted in two soils, the plants in the darker soil grew taller. The darker soil held more water after each watering, and the two plots received the same light and the same number of seeds.

The results best support which conclusion?
options: Darker soil is always better for tomatoes.
Under these conditions, the darker soil's water retention accompanied taller growth.
Tomatoes need no light to grow.
hints: Note exactly what was held constant and what differed.
Same variety, same light; the soils differed, and water retention was observed.
The supported claim stays inside those conditions.
expl: With variety and light equal, the darker soil — which held more water — accompanied taller growth under these conditions. Choice B claims no more than that.

q:
The mayor's plan to widen the avenue was, to its supporters, a simple matter of arithmetic: more lanes, more cars moved. Its opponents kept returning to a stubborn observation — every widening of the avenue in living memory had, within three years, filled to the same congestion as before, as drivers who had avoided the avenue returned to it.

The opponents' observation is offered primarily to
options: prove that cars should be banned from the avenue
suggest that widening may not relieve congestion for long
explain why the mayor proposed the plan
show that traffic has decreased over time
hints: What pattern do the opponents cite?
Each past widening refilled to the same congestion within three years.
A repeating pattern undercuts the plan's expected benefit.
expl: Past widenings refilled to the same congestion, which suggests the new widening may likewise fail to relieve congestion for long — a doubt about durability, not a call for a ban.

q:
Running a marathon in under three hours was, for decades, a mark of the elite amateur. In a single recent year, more than four thousand ordinary club runners broke it, a change coaches attribute less to training than to shoes: modern racing shoes return a portion of each stride's energy to the runner.

According to the passage, the recent change is attributed mainly to
hints: The passage assigns the cause itself — find its wording.
Coaches attribute the change 'less to training than to shoes'.
The stated cause is the shoes' energy return.
expl: The passage says coaches credit the shoes — which return part of each stride's energy — more than training. That is the stated attribution.

q:
Neither of the two bridges that serve the island _____ older than forty years, a fact that surprises visitors who assume the crossings are historic.

Which verb form correctly completes the sentence?
hints: 'Neither' as a subject is singular.
The verb must agree with 'neither', not with 'bridges'.
A present-tense singular form fits the fact being stated.
expl: 'Neither' is singular, so the verb is 'is' — the plural noun inside the following phrase does not govern agreement.

q:
Paragraph: 'To can a vegetable safely, the jar must be sealed while its contents are hot enough to drive out air; as the jar cools, the remaining air contracts and pulls the lid tight. The seal, not the recipe, is what stands between a pantry shelf and a dangerous one.'

Which heading best fits the paragraph?
options: The Seal Is the Safety: How a Cooling Jar Protects Its Contents
hints: What single mechanism does the paragraph explain?
Cooling contracts the air and pulls the lid tight — the seal.
The heading should name that mechanism and its stakes.
expl: The paragraph explains how the cooling jar creates the seal and why the seal is the safety-critical step — heading B. It gives no recipes and no history.

q:
The word arrived in English by a curious road: a Persian term for a checked pattern, carried west by traders, narrowed in chess to the moment a king is threatened, and narrowed again in banking to a written order for payment. Each stop on the road kept the pattern and changed the stakes.

As used in the passage, the final sentence suggests that the word's history shows
options: meanings drifting randomly with no pattern
a core image persisting while its applications changed
hints: Track what stayed constant across the stops.
The checked pattern persisted; the fields of use changed.
Persistence of image plus change of application is the point.
expl: At every stop the checked-pattern image persisted while the application — cloth, chess, banking — changed; the sentence summarizes exactly that persistence-through-change.

q:
A coastal town rebuilt its seawall two feet higher after the flood year. In the decade since, no storm has topped it. The town's engineer refuses to call the wall a success, though: 'We have not been tested,' she says, 'by anything like the flood year.'

The engineer's refusal rests on the reasoning that
options: the wall is certainly too low
an untested defense has not yet demonstrated it can succeed
storms have become stronger every year
the town should not have rebuilt the wall
hints: What evidence would the engineer accept?
A storm comparable to the flood year has not occurred since.
Absence of failure without a real test is not proof of success.
expl: No storm like the flood year has tested the wall, so its success is undemonstrated rather than proven — the engineer's exact caution.

q:
The lecture hall's acoustics were designed for speech. _____ a string quartet that performed there last spring sounded strangely distant, as if playing from behind a curtain.

Which transition best completes the sentence?
hints: The second sentence pushes against the first's implication.
Designed well for speech — yet music sounded distant.
A result that runs against expectation takes a concessive transition.
expl: The distant sound contrasts with the hall's careful design, so the concessive 'Even so,' fits; result and addition transitions point the wrong way.

q:
In one district, students who practiced arithmetic facts for ten minutes daily gained, over a term, twice the fluency of a matched group that practiced for thirty minutes once a week. Total practice time was nearly equal; only its distribution differed.

Which conclusion is best supported by the study as described?
options: Longer weekly sessions are always superior.
With total time nearly equal, shorter daily practice accompanied greater fluency gains.
hints: Hold total time steady in your mind — it was nearly equal.
What differed was distribution: daily versus weekly.
The gain followed the daily distribution.
expl: Total time was nearly equal, so the difference tracks the distribution: short daily practice accompanied twice the fluency gain. Preference was never measured.

According to the shopkeeper, which frames are ready now?
hints: The speaker distinguishes the sets by their status.
Oak: ready. Walnut: still at the finisher's.
Only one set is described as ready.

q:
When the printing press reached a new town, its first products were rarely books. Printers earned their keep on the small and urgent: notices, forms, advertisements, and single-sheet announcements — work that had to be remade constantly and could not wait for a scribe.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Books were unpopular in new towns.
A press's early business was everyday job printing, not books, because that work was constant and urgent.
hints: Ask what filled the printer's order book and why.
Small, urgent, constantly remade work — notices and forms.
The reason given is constancy and urgency.
expl: The passage says printers lived on small urgent jobs that recurred constantly, while books were rare at first — choice B states both the fact and the reason.

q:
City crews planted rows of young maples along the avenue last spring. Within a year, summer temperatures on the shaded blocks measured several degrees cooler than on nearby unshaded streets, and shopkeepers reported that more pedestrians lingered outside their stores.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Planting trees is too expensive for most cities.
Newly planted street trees cooled the avenue and drew more foot traffic.
Maples grow faster than other street trees.
hints: Look for the choice that covers both effects mentioned.
The passage reports two results: cooler temperatures and more lingering pedestrians.
Reject choices that add claims the passage never makes.
expl: Both reported effects — cooling and increased foot traffic — appear in the passage. The other choices invent claims (cost, growth rate, shopkeeper preference) that the text never states.

q:
The library's evening hours were extended in September. By November, staff noticed that the study rooms filled with high-school students after dinner — a group that had rarely used the library on school nights before the change.

Which inference is best supported by the passage?
options: Extending evening hours made the library usable for students after dinner.
Study rooms were built in September.
hints: An inference must be supported by what the passage actually reports.
Connect the timing: hours changed in September; a new pattern appeared by November.
Avoid choices that guess at motives the passage never mentions.
expl: The sequence supports the inference: once hours extended into the evening, students began using the study rooms after dinner. Motives (disliking home) and constructions (rooms built) are not in the text.

The committee released its report on Tuesday; it recommended three changes.

The subject is 'section' — the phrase 'along with its conductor' does not make it plural.
A singular subject takes a singular verb.
expl: The subject is the singular 'section'; phrases set off by 'along with' do not change the subject's number. The singular verb 'is' agrees.

q:
Bees communicate the location of flowers through a 'waggle dance' performed inside the hive. The angle of the dance relative to the sun tells watching bees the direction of the food source, while the dance's duration signals how far away it is.

According to the passage, the duration of the waggle dance communicates
hints: Match each detail to what the passage assigns to it.
Angle handles one thing; duration handles another.
The passage separates direction (angle) from distance (duration).
expl: The passage states plainly that duration signals distance, while angle signals direction. The other options are not assigned to duration anywhere in the text.

q:
A school garden club tracked its tomato plants for a month. Plants watered every other day grew taller than plants watered daily, which surprised the students, who had expected more water to mean more growth.

Which statement is best supported by the passage?
options: Tomatoes should never be watered daily.
In this club's month of tracking, less frequent watering coincided with taller plants.
hints: Stay inside what was actually observed: one club, one month.
Strong words like 'never' and 'kills' go beyond the evidence.
The supported claim is narrow: in this observation, the every-other-day plants grew taller.
expl: The passage reports one club's one-month observation. Only option B keeps that narrow scope; the others turn a single observation into universal rules the text never makes.

q:
When the factory switched to LED lighting, managers expected only lower electricity bills. Within months, however, supervisors also reported fewer errors on the night shift — a benefit nobody had predicted.

The author's purpose in the final clause — 'a benefit nobody had predicted' — is most likely to
options: emphasize that the second benefit was unexpected
hints: Ask why the author included this detail, not just what it says.
The sentence contrasts the expected benefit with the one that surprised everyone.
Purpose questions reward the function of the words in the passage.
expl: The clause underscores surprise: lower bills were expected, fewer errors were not. The author is emphasizing the unexpected bonus, not criticizing anyone or changing the subject.

q:
Despite the forecast of rain, the hikers set out early. By noon the sky had cleared, and the trail — muddy but passable — led them to the summit before the light faded.

As used in the passage, 'passable' most nearly means
hints: Use the surrounding action: the hikers used the trail and reached the summit.
Muddy 'but' passable — the word is contrasted with the mud, then they walked it.
Choose the meaning the sentence's own events prove.
expl: The hikers traveled the trail to the summit, so 'passable' must mean able to be traveled on — muddy, but usable. The context rules out the other meanings.

q:
In an experiment, two identical seedlings were placed in the same soil and light. One received plain water; the other received water mixed with a small amount of fertilizer. After three weeks, the fertilized seedling was noticeably taller.

Which question does this experiment best help answer?
options: Which soil is best for seedlings?
How much light do seedlings need?
hints: Find the one thing that differed between the two seedlings.
Soil and light were held the same; only the fertilizer changed.
An experiment answers questions about the variable it changes.
expl: Only one variable differed — fertilizer — so the experiment tests fertilizer's effect on growth. Soil, light, and water questions can't be answered because those were kept the same.

q:
A survey of 400 shoppers found that 62% choose a store mainly for its prices, 23% for its location, and 15% for its product selection.

Which conclusion is best supported by the survey?
options: Most shoppers rank product selection first.
Price is the most common main reason shoppers in this survey chose a store.
All shoppers care only about price.
hints: Let the largest percentage speak, and keep the claim inside the survey.
62% is a majority, and it belongs to prices.
Avoid absolutes ('never', 'all', 'only') the data doesn't support.
expl: With 62%, price is the most-cited main reason among these 400 shoppers. The other options contradict the data or stretch it into absolutes.

q:
(Transcript) Professor: 'Most students assume the desert tortoise survives the summer by finding shade. In fact, it survives by spending the hottest months underground, in burrows where the temperature stays far cooler than the surface.'

What does the professor mainly correct?
options: The idea that tortoises live in deserts
The assumption that shade is the tortoise's main survival strategy
The claim that burrows are cool
The belief that summers are hot
hints: Listen for the contrast: 'assume' versus 'in fact.'
The professor replaces one explanation with another.
Shade is the assumed strategy; burrows are the real one.
expl: The professor's 'in fact' corrects the assumption: shade is not the main strategy — underground burrows are. The other options are things the professor accepts, not corrects.

q:
(Transcript) Caller: 'I'd like to book the hall for Saturday the 14th — sorry, Saturday the 21st — for about fifty guests.'

According to the caller, the booking is for
hints: Speakers correct themselves; the final version is the answer.
The caller replaces the 14th with a new date.
Write down the corrected information, not the first version.
expl: The caller self-corrects from the 14th to the 21st. Listening tests plant these corrections constantly; the last stated version is the booking.

q:
Paragraph: 'Early attempts to build a flying machine failed for a simple reason: inventors copied the shape of birds without understanding the forces that keep a craft in the air. Only when researchers studied lift itself — measuring how air moves over a curved wing — did practical designs begin to appear.'

Which heading best fits the paragraph?
options: Early Setbacks Point Toward the Science of Lift
How to Build a Wing at Home
hints: A heading states the paragraph's whole gist, not one detail.
The paragraph moves from failed copying to studying lift.
Reject headings that are too broad, too narrow, or off-topic.
expl: The paragraph's arc is failure-through-copying followed by progress through understanding lift — exactly what heading B says. The others miss the arc or invent content.

q:
When the city replaced its diesel buses with electric ones, the transit director expected quieter streets. Within a year, however, mechanics reported something else: the electric buses needed far less brake work, because their motors slowed the vehicles by recovering energy instead of grinding pads.

The author's mention of brake work primarily serves to
options: argue that buses should be free
hints: Look for what the sentence adds beyond the expected point.
The director expected quieter streets; brake savings were not part of that expectation.
An added, unplanned advantage is an additional benefit.
expl: The passage sets up one expected gain (quieter streets) and then presents brake savings as a further, unexpected gain — an additional benefit, not a criticism or a mechanics lesson.

q: A class has boys and girls in the ratio 2:3, with 40 students in total. How many boys are there? (Boys are the first number in the ratio.)
hints: Add the ratio parts to find how many parts share the total.
Total parts = 2 + 3 = 5, so each part = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 students.
Boys hold 2 parts: 2 × 8.
expl: Each part = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 students. Boys = 2 × 8 = 16.

q: A circle has radius 9. What is its area, in terms of π?
hints: Area of a circle is π times the radius squared.
Square the radius: 9² = 81.
Don't confuse area (r²) with circumference (2r).
expl: A = πr² = π × 9² = 81π.

q: Which expression equals 5^3 × 5^3?
hints: Same base, multiplied: add the exponents.
Then evaluate 5^6.
expl: Add exponents for the same base: 5^6 = 15,625.

q: A circle has radius 8. What is its area, in terms of π?
hints: Area of a circle is π times the radius squared.
Square the radius: 8² = 64.
Don't confuse area (r²) with circumference (2r).
expl: A = πr² = π × 8² = 64π.

q: A class has boys and girls in the ratio 4:2, with 42 students in total. How many boys are there? (Boys are the first number in the ratio.)
hints: Add the ratio parts to find how many parts share the total.
Total parts = 4 + 2 = 6, so each part = 42 ÷ 6 = 7 students.
Boys hold 4 parts: 4 × 7.
expl: Each part = 42 ÷ 6 = 7 students. Boys = 4 × 7 = 28.

q: What is the slope of the line through (3, 3) and (4, 6)?
hints: Slope is rise over run: change in y divided by change in x.
Change in y = 6 − 3 = 3; change in x = 4 − 3 = 1.
Divide 3 by 1.

q: What is the slope of the line through (1, 0) and (2, 1)?
hints: Slope is rise over run: change in y divided by change in x.
Change in y = 1 − 0 = 1; change in x = 2 − 1 = 1.
Divide 1 by 1.

q: Which expression equals 2^4 × 2^2?
hints: Same base, multiplied: add the exponents.
Then evaluate 2^6.
expl: Add exponents for the same base: 2^6 = 64.

q: If f(x) = 3x² − 1x + 3, what is f(5)?
hints: Substitute 5 everywhere you see x.
3(5)² means 3 × 25. Watch the minus sign on the middle term.
Compute each term separately, then combine.

q: A bag holds 3 red and 5 blue marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is the probability it is red?
hints: Probability = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
Total marbles = 3 + 5 = 8.
Simplify the fraction if you can.

q: A circle has radius 7. What is its area, in terms of π?
hints: Area of a circle is π times the radius squared.
Square the radius: 7² = 49.
Don't confuse area (r²) with circumference (2r).
expl: A = πr² = π × 7² = 49π.

q: A class has boys and girls in the ratio 6:5, with 66 students in total. How many boys are there? (Boys are the first number in the ratio.)
hints: Add the ratio parts to find how many parts share the total.
Total parts = 6 + 5 = 11, so each part = 66 ÷ 11 = 6 students.
Boys hold 6 parts: 6 × 6.
expl: Each part = 66 ÷ 11 = 6 students. Boys = 6 × 6 = 36.

q: If 3x + y = 29 and x − y = 7, what is the value of x?
hints: The y terms cancel if you add the two equations.
Adding: 3x + x = 29 + 7.
So 4x = 36. Divide.
expl: Add the equations to eliminate y: 4x = 36, so x = 9. (Then y = 2, which checks in both equations.)

q: A circle has radius 4. What is its area, in terms of π?
hints: Area of a circle is π times the radius squared.
Square the radius: 4² = 16.
Don't confuse area (r²) with circumference (2r).
expl: A = πr² = π × 4² = 16π.

q: If f(x) = 2x² − 8x + 1, what is f(2)?
hints: Substitute 2 everywhere you see x.
2(2)² means 2 × 4. Watch the minus sign on the middle term.
Compute each term separately, then combine.

q: A geometric sequence begins 3, 6, 12, 24… What is the 9th term?
hints: Find the common ratio first.
Each term multiplies by 2; the 9th term uses the ratio 8 times.
Term n = 3 × 2^8.

q:
A bakery that once sold only white and wheat loaves began offering rye, sourdough, and seeded varieties. Sales rose — but not, the owner admits, because customers suddenly preferred those breads. Most buyers still choose white; they simply visit more often now that the shop feels like a place where they might find something new.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Customers have stopped buying white bread.
A wider selection can raise sales by drawing customers in more often, even when their favorites stay the same.
Sourdough is the bakery's best-selling loaf.
Small bakeries cannot compete with large ones.
hints: Find the sentence that explains why sales rose.
The owner says favorites did not change; visits did.
The main idea must cover both the wider shelves and the unchanged favorites.
expl: Sales rose because variety brought customers through the door more often, while their actual favorite — white bread — stayed the same. Only choice B captures both halves of that point.

q:
To the relief of the night staff, the hospital's new scheduling software proved tractable: within a week, even the least technical nurses were building their own rotas without help.

As used in the passage, 'tractable' most nearly means
hints: The staff mastered the software within a week.
A thing people can handle easily is manageable.
Match the word to the outcome described: quick, unaided use.
expl: The nurses used the software on their own within a week, so 'tractable' here means easy to manage. The other choices contradict or ignore that outcome.

q:
The museum extended its hours on Fridays. _____ attendance on Friday evenings doubled within two months.

Which transition best completes the sentence?
hints: Name the relationship between the two facts.
Longer hours came first; higher attendance followed from them.
A following effect is signalled by a result transition.
expl: The doubled attendance is the effect of the extended hours, so the result transition 'As a result,' is the logical fit.

q:
Neither the coach nor the players _____ aware of the schedule change until the morning of the game.

Which verb form correctly completes the sentence?
hints: With 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.
The nearer subject here is 'players', which is plural.
The sentence is set in the past ('until the morning of the game'), so choose the plural past form.
expl: With neither/nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'players' (plural), and the past-tense setting ('until the morning of the game') requires 'were'.

q:
In a trial of two compost mixtures, researchers kept soil, water, and sunlight identical for forty tomato plants. The twenty plants fed mixture B produced, on average, 18 percent more fruit by weight than the twenty fed mixture A.

The results of the trial best support which conclusion?
options: Mixture B caused the higher yield under the trial's conditions.
Mixture A is poisonous to plants.
hints: Every condition except the mixture was held the same.
When only one variable differs, a difference in outcome points to that variable.
The claim must stay inside the trial's conditions.
expl: Because soil, water, and sunlight were identical, the yield difference is attributable to the mixtures — and the supported claim stays within those trial conditions.

q:
(Transcript) Manager: 'Before we approve the budget, note that the figures on page two are last year's. The updated totals are in the appendix, and they are slightly higher.'

According to the manager, where are the current budget figures?
hints: The manager corrects an assumption about page two.
Page two holds last year's figures.
The updated totals are named directly: the appendix.
expl: The manager says page two is out of date and the updated totals are in the appendix — a direct statement, not an inference.

q:
Paragraph: 'Before the telegraph, news of a battle might take weeks to cross an ocean, and by the time it arrived it was history. The telegraph collapsed that distance to minutes, and newspapers began competing not on what had happened but on how quickly they could say it.'

Which heading best fits the paragraph?
options: Famous Battles of the Nineteenth Century
How the Telegraph Changed the Speed of News
hints: A heading must cover the whole arc: before, then after.
The paragraph is about speed, not battles or instructions.
The telegraph's effect on news timing is the through-line.
expl: The paragraph contrasts slow news before the telegraph with minutes-fast news after it — a change in the speed of news. The other headings are too narrow or off-topic.

q:
Farmers in the valley had long planted a single variety of potato. When a blight arrived in 2019, fields planted with that variety failed almost completely, while the few farms that had kept three or four varieties lost only the susceptible rows.

It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
options: planting several varieties reduced the farms' total losses
the valley now grows no potatoes
hints: Compare the outcomes of the two planting strategies.
Single-variety fields failed almost completely; varied farms lost only some rows.
An inference must stay close to that comparison.
expl: The varied farms lost only the susceptible rows while single-variety fields failed almost completely, so variety reduced total losses. The passage does not support the stronger or unrelated claims.

q:
The trail guide warns that the last mile of the canyon path is exposed, with no shade and no water. Hikers _____ begin that stretch before noon in summer.

Which choice best completes the sentence with the meaning the guide intends?
hints: Connect the warning to the advice it implies.
No shade and no water at midday is a hazard.
The intended meaning is caution about timing.
expl: A warning about heat exposure implies hikers should not start the exposed stretch at midday; choice A carries that caution.

q:
A library system noticed that books displayed face-out on the ends of shelves were borrowed three times as often as the same books shelved spine-out. The librarians changed nothing else — not the collection, not the hours — only the orientation of a few hundred covers.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Face-out displays increased borrowing of the same books.
Borrowing has declined in recent years.
hints: Only one thing changed; one result followed.
Same books, same hours — only orientation differed.
The main idea links that single change to the borrowing result.
expl: With everything else held constant, rotating covers face-out tripled borrowing of the identical books. That change-and-result pair is the main idea.

q: Which option is correct?
options: The committee released its findings on Friday, it recommended three changes to the admissions process.
The committee released its findings on Friday; it recommended three changes to the admissions process.
The committee released its findings on Friday recommended three changes to the admissions process.
The committee released its findings on Friday. Recommended three changes to the admissions process.
hints: The sentence joins two complete thoughts.
A comma alone cannot join them — that is a comma splice.
A semicolon joins two complete, related thoughts correctly.
expl: The original joins two independent clauses with only a comma. The semicolon version joins them correctly; the others keep the splice, drop punctuation, or create a fragment.

q:
Beekeepers in the region lost a third of their hives in a single winter. Surveys found no single cause: a parasite weakened the colonies, a late frost caught them short of stores, and a wet autumn had kept bees from foraging on the last warm days.

According to the passage, the hive losses resulted from
hints: The passage explicitly rejects a single cause.
Count the stresses it lists: parasite, frost, wet autumn.
Together, not alone, is the passage's answer.
expl: The passage names three stresses — parasite, late frost, and a wet autumn — and says there was no single cause, so the losses came from several stresses together.

q:
When the factory moved its start time from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m., supervisors braced for complaints from the early crew. _____, the early crew asked to keep the new time: the extra hour of sleep, several said, was worth more than the earlier finish.

Which transition best completes the sentence?
hints: What was expected, and what actually happened?
Complaints were expected; approval happened instead.
An outcome opposite to expectation takes a contrast transition.
expl: The crew's approval contradicts the expected complaints, so the contrast transition 'In contrast,' fits the turn.

q:
The old bridge was, by every engineering measure, obsolete — too narrow for modern traffic, costly to maintain, and due for replacement. Yet when demolition was proposed, the town council chamber filled with residents who had crossed it on foot every day of their lives and could not imagine the river without it.

The author includes the residents' reaction most likely to
options: prove the bridge was well engineered
show that a structure's value is not measured only in engineering terms
argue that councils should never replace bridges
explain how demolition is carried out
hints: Weigh the two halves of the passage against each other.
The first half measures the bridge by engineering; the second measures it by daily life.
The reaction introduces a different kind of value.
expl: The passage contrasts engineering measures with the bridge's place in residents' daily lives, showing value beyond engineering terms — without claiming demolition is never right.

q:
A survey of 900 commuters found that 48 percent would accept a longer commute for a quieter train car, 31 percent for a guaranteed seat, and 21 percent for faster Wi-Fi.

Which conclusion is best supported by the survey?
options: Quiet was the most common first priority among the options offered.
Commutes are getting longer every year.
hints: Compare the three percentages directly.
48 percent is larger than 31 and 21.
The largest share named quiet — first among the offered options.
expl: Quiet drew 48 percent, the largest share of the three options, so it was the most common priority among those offered. The passage says nothing about trends over time.

q:
(Transcript) Librarian: 'The reading room closes at eight tonight, not nine — we're hosting the school awards in there from seven thirty, so please gather your things by seven fifteen.'

According to the librarian, by what time should readers gather their things?
hints: Several times are mentioned; find the one attached to gathering things.
Eight is closing; seven thirty is the awards start.
The instruction says 'by seven fifteen'.
expl: The librarian gives three times, but the gathering instruction is explicit: 'by seven fifteen.' The other options attach to closing and the event start.

q:
The library's evening hours were extended in September. By November, staff noticed that the study rooms filled with high-school students after dinner — a group that had rarely used the library on school nights before the change.

Which inference is best supported by the passage?
options: Extending evening hours made the library usable for students after dinner.
Study rooms were built in September.
hints: An inference must be supported by what the passage actually reports.
Connect the timing: hours changed in September; a new pattern appeared by November.
Avoid choices that guess at motives the passage never mentions.
expl: The sequence supports the inference: once hours extended into the evening, students began using the study rooms after dinner. Motives (disliking home) and constructions (rooms built) are not in the text.

q:
Even with a comfortable income, Marta remained frugal, mending clothes, planning meals around sales, and keeping her old car long after she could have replaced it.

As used in the passage, 'frugal' most nearly means
hints: The examples after the word explain it.
Mending, planning around sales, keeping an old car — what habit do they share?
The word describes how she handles money, not how much she has.
expl: Every example shows care in spending: mending instead of buying, planning around sales, keeping the old car. 'Frugal' means careful with money — not careless, and not simply wealthy.

q:
The bridge inspection found serious corrosion. _____, the city closed the bridge to all traffic the following week.

Which transition best completes the sentence?
hints: Decide the relationship: does the second sentence contrast, exemplify, follow from, or resemble the first?
The closure happened because of what the inspection found.
Cause first, effect second — pick the transition that signals consequence.
expl: 'As a result' signals that the closure followed from the inspection's findings. 'Nevertheless' needs a contrast, 'For example' an illustration, 'Similarly' a comparison — none fits.

q:
Paragraph: 'Coral reefs occupy a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. The reef's structure — built by colonies of small animals over centuries — creates the crevices, shade, and currents that so many other species depend on.'

Which heading best fits the paragraph?
options: The Largest Animals in the Ocean
Small Area, Immense Shelter: Why Reefs Hold So Much Life
How to Build an Artificial Reef
hints: The heading must match both the small size and the large effect.
The paragraph explains why so much life gathers there: structure.
Only one heading carries the size-versus-life contrast.
expl: The paragraph's point is the contrast between the reefs' tiny area and the quarter of marine species they shelter, explained by their structure — exactly what heading B states.

q:
Unlike her colleagues, who announced each result the moment it appeared, Dr. Osei was reticent about her experiment, saying only that 'the work is not finished' until the final trial had been replicated twice.

As used in the passage, 'reticent' most nearly means
hints: Contrast her behavior with her colleagues'.
They announced at once; she said almost nothing until the end.
Speaking little, by choice, is reluctance to speak.
expl: Dr. Osei withheld comment until replication was complete, in contrast to colleagues who announced immediately — 'reticent' means reluctant to speak.

q:
A town that switched its streetlights to warmer, dimmer bulbs reported two changes the following year: energy costs fell by a fifth, and residents' complaints about glare dropped sharply. Astronomers at the nearby observatory, the council minutes note, sent a letter of thanks.

It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
options: the dimmer bulbs also improved conditions for observing the sky
the town removed all its streetlights
energy costs rose after the switch
hints: Ask why the astronomers would write in thanks.
Dimmer, warmer light means less light spilling into the sky.
Their thanks implies the change helped their work.
expl: Astronomers benefit from reduced sky glow, so their letter of thanks implies the dimmer bulbs improved observing conditions. The other choices contradict the passage.

q:
Before the reservoir was built, the river flooded the lower fields almost every spring. The floods ruined some plantings, but old farmers spoke of them with a kind of gratitude: each flood left behind a layer of dark silt, and the fields that flooded most were, in the dry years, the fields that yielded best.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The reservoir ended all farming in the valley.
The spring floods were both a harm and, through the silt they left, a lasting benefit to the fields.
Farmers preferred floods to droughts in all cases.
Silt is the only fertilizer the fields ever needed.
hints: Hold both sides of the farmers' attitude at once.
Floods ruined plantings — and enriched the soil.
The main idea must include the harm and the benefit.
expl: The passage balances ruined plantings against silt-fed yields in dry years: the floods harmed and benefited the same fields. Choice B is the only one holding both.

q:
The orchestra's conductor, together with the soloists, _____ honored at the reception after the performance.

Which verb form correctly completes the sentence?
hints: A phrase set off by commas does not change the subject.
The subject is 'conductor' — singular.
'Together with the soloists' is an aside, not part of the subject.
expl: The subject is the singular 'conductor'; 'together with the soloists' is parenthetical and does not make it plural. The past setting requires 'was'.

q:
A pediatric clinic replaced its paper appointment reminders with text messages. Missed appointments fell by a quarter in six months. The clinic's director is careful about the credit, though: the same six months saw the clinic hire a second receptionist, whose calls may have done part of the work.

The director's caution is based on the fact that
options: text messages are unpopular with patients
another change happened at the same time, so the texts may not deserve all the credit
the receptionist opposed the text system
hints: What else changed during the same period?
A second receptionist was hired and made calls.
Two changes at once make it impossible to credit one alone.
expl: Because the receptionist's calls began in the same period as the texts, the fall in missed appointments cannot be credited to the texts alone — the basis of the director's caution.

q:
The hikers reached the ridge at noon. _____ they could see the whole valley, including the river bend they had crossed at dawn.

Which transition best completes the sentence?
hints: What does the second sentence do?
It describes the view from the place just reached.
A location phrase links the arrival to the view.
expl: 'From there' ties the view directly to the ridge they reached; the other transitions signal contrast, concession, or example, none of which fits.

q:
The report runs to three hundred pages, but its argument can be stated in one sentence: a city's bus network succeeds or fails on frequency — whether a rider can trust that a bus will come soon — far more than on the comfort of the buses themselves.

As used in the passage, 'frequency' most nearly means
hints: The passage defines the word by its own explanation.
It glosses the term as trusting 'a bus will come soon'.
Coming soon, repeatedly, is a matter of how often.
expl: The passage explains frequency as whether 'a bus will come soon' — that is, how often buses run. The other meanings ignore the passage's own gloss.

q:
In a study of office plants, employees in rooms with two potted plants reported headaches 12 percent less often over a month than employees in identical rooms without plants. Air monitors showed no measurable difference between the rooms.

Which conclusion is best supported by the study as described?
options: Plants cleaned the air in the offices.
Headache reports differed between the rooms, though the study does not show that air quality caused it.
Offices should replace monitors with plants.
Headaches are caused by office work.
hints: Separate what was measured from what was merely assumed.
Headache reports differed; air readings did not.
A supported conclusion cannot claim a cause the monitors ruled unmeasured.
expl: The only measured differences are in headache reports; air monitors showed no difference, so claiming plants cleaned the air goes beyond the study. Choice B stays inside the evidence.

q:
(Transcript) Coach: 'Saturday's session moves to the indoor court — the roof work on the main gym starts Friday, so bring shoes for the hard floor, not the track.'

According to the coach, why does Saturday's session move indoors?
options: Roof work begins on the main gym.
The hard floor is better for training.
hints: Find the reason the coach states, in order.
The roof work is named as the cause; shoes are an instruction.
Do not trade the stated cause for a detail that follows it.
expl: The coach states the cause directly: roof work starts Friday on the main gym. The shoes are a consequence to prepare for, not the reason for the move.

q:
Paragraph: 'A lighthouse does not move, yet it guides moving ships; its whole usefulness is in being exactly where the charts say it is. When a light was misplaced on a chart by even a mile, the error could wreck the very ships the light existed to save.'

Which heading best fits the paragraph?
options: A Fixed Light, A Fatal Error: Accuracy in Navigation
hints: The paragraph's tension is between fixedness and error.
A correctly charted light saves; a misplaced one wrecks.
The heading must carry the accuracy theme.
expl: The paragraph turns on chart accuracy — a fixed light whose position is wrongly charted becomes a danger. Heading B captures that; the others are general topics the paragraph does not develop.

q:
The town's annual fair had always been organized by the agricultural society. This year the society's longtime secretary retired, and no replacement volunteered. _____ the fair was cancelled for the first time in sixty years.

Which transition best completes the sentence?
hints: Trace the chain from the retirement to the cancellation.
No secretary and no volunteer led directly to the cancellation.
A direct consequence takes a result transition.
expl: The cancellation follows directly from the unfilled secretary post, so the result transition 'As a result,' expresses the relationship.

q:
Small as it is, the island's post office functions as far more than a place to send letters. It is where ferry schedules are posted, where lost dogs are announced, and where, on storm days, the postmaster reads the weather report aloud to whoever is waiting for the mail boat.

The author mentions the ferry schedules and lost dogs most likely to
options: show the range of roles the post office plays in island life
argue that mail service should be expanded
explain how weather reports are produced
hints: Ask what the examples have in common.
Each example is a service beyond sending letters.
A list of unlike services shows breadth of role.
expl: Schedules, lost-dog notices, and weather readings are all roles beyond mail — the examples demonstrate how much of island life runs through the post office.

q:
Records from the mill show that in 1910 a weaver tended four looms. By 1930, with the arrival of automatic loaders, a weaver tended sixteen. Output per weaver rose sharply — but so, the records note, did the number of weavers the mill employed, because cloth that had been a luxury became cheap enough for ordinary households.

According to the passage, employment at the mill rose because
options: weavers became slower at their work
cheaper cloth widened the market for it
hints: Follow the passage's own chain: loaders, then cheaper cloth, then what?
Cheaper cloth reached ordinary households.
A wider market needs more cloth — and more weavers.
expl: The passage links rising employment to demand: automation made cloth affordable to ordinary households, widening the market faster than it reduced labor per yard.

q:
The recipe's first printing called for a 'moderate oven,' a phrase that meant something precise to cooks who banked coal fires and meaningless to their grandchildren, who set dials. When the book was reissued, the editor rendered such phrases into degrees — and, some readers complained, edited a small piece of the past out of the book.

It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
options: the grandchildren could not cook at all
'moderate oven' once carried information that a dial setting only partly replaces
coal fires were more accurate than dials
hints: What did the old phrase hold that the new one may not?
It belonged to a whole practice of judging heat by hand and fire.
The complaint suggests something was lost in translation.
expl: The old phrase was precise within its own practice, and readers felt the conversion lost something — so the term carried information a number only partly replaces.

q:
The two candidates for the scholarship had nearly identical grades. What separated them, the committee chair said afterward, was the essay: one listed achievements, while the other showed, through a single summer's work, how a failing community garden was brought back — and what the writer learned when the first plantings died.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Grades are unimportant in scholarship decisions.
When records are equal, a vivid account of real work — including its failures — can be what distinguishes a candidate.
hints: Start from what the chair says actually separated them.
The essays differed in kind: a list versus a story of work and failure.
The main idea must be about that difference, not about grades alone.
expl: With grades equal, the committee was swayed by the essay that showed real work and honest failure over a bare list — choice B states exactly that.

q:
(Transcript) Student: 'I turned in the form for the science fair on Tuesday — sorry, on Thursday — the day the office reopened after the storm.'

According to the student, the form was turned in on
options: the day before the office reopened
hints: The speaker corrects herself mid-sentence.
The correction replaces Tuesday with Thursday.
A self-correction means the second version is the claim.
expl: The student corrects 'Tuesday' to 'Thursday' — in these items the corrected version is the answer, and the office detail confirms the day.

q:
When seeds of the same tomato variety were planted in two soils, the plants in the darker soil grew taller. The darker soil held more water after each watering, and the two plots received the same light and the same number of seeds.

The results best support which conclusion?
options: Darker soil is always better for tomatoes.
Under these conditions, the darker soil's water retention accompanied taller growth.
Tomatoes need no light to grow.
hints: Note exactly what was held constant and what differed.
Same variety, same light; the soils differed, and water retention was observed.
The supported claim stays inside those conditions.
expl: With variety and light equal, the darker soil — which held more water — accompanied taller growth under these conditions. Choice B claims no more than that.

q:
The mayor's plan to widen the avenue was, to its supporters, a simple matter of arithmetic: more lanes, more cars moved. Its opponents kept returning to a stubborn observation — every widening of the avenue in living memory had, within three years, filled to the same congestion as before, as drivers who had avoided the avenue returned to it.

The opponents' observation is offered primarily to
options: prove that cars should be banned from the avenue
suggest that widening may not relieve congestion for long
explain why the mayor proposed the plan
show that traffic has decreased over time
hints: What pattern do the opponents cite?
Each past widening refilled to the same congestion within three years.
A repeating pattern undercuts the plan's expected benefit.
expl: Past widenings refilled to the same congestion, which suggests the new widening may likewise fail to relieve congestion for long — a doubt about durability, not a call for a ban.

q:
Running a marathon in under three hours was, for decades, a mark of the elite amateur. In a single recent year, more than four thousand ordinary club runners broke it, a change coaches attribute less to training than to shoes: modern racing shoes return a portion of each stride's energy to the runner.

According to the passage, the recent change is attributed mainly to
hints: The passage assigns the cause itself — find its wording.
Coaches attribute the change 'less to training than to shoes'.
The stated cause is the shoes' energy return.
expl: The passage says coaches credit the shoes — which return part of each stride's energy — more than training. That is the stated attribution.

q:
Neither of the two bridges that serve the island _____ older than forty years, a fact that surprises visitors who assume the crossings are historic.

Which verb form correctly completes the sentence?
hints: 'Neither' as a subject is singular.
The verb must agree with 'neither', not with 'bridges'.
A present-tense singular form fits the fact being stated.
expl: 'Neither' is singular, so the verb is 'is' — the plural noun inside the following phrase does not govern agreement.

q:
Paragraph: 'To can a vegetable safely, the jar must be sealed while its contents are hot enough to drive out air; as the jar cools, the remaining air contracts and pulls the lid tight. The seal, not the recipe, is what stands between a pantry shelf and a dangerous one.'

Which heading best fits the paragraph?
options: The Seal Is the Safety: How a Cooling Jar Protects Its Contents
hints: What single mechanism does the paragraph explain?
Cooling contracts the air and pulls the lid tight — the seal.
The heading should name that mechanism and its stakes.
expl: The paragraph explains how the cooling jar creates the seal and why the seal is the safety-critical step — heading B. It gives no recipes and no history.

q:
The word arrived in English by a curious road: a Persian term for a checked pattern, carried west by traders, narrowed in chess to the moment a king is threatened, and narrowed again in banking to a written order for payment. Each stop on the road kept the pattern and changed the stakes.

As used in the passage, the final sentence suggests that the word's history shows
options: meanings drifting randomly with no pattern
a core image persisting while its applications changed
hints: Track what stayed constant across the stops.
The checked pattern persisted; the fields of use changed.
Persistence of image plus change of application is the point.
expl: At every stop the checked-pattern image persisted while the application — cloth, chess, banking — changed; the sentence summarizes exactly that persistence-through-change.

q:
A coastal town rebuilt its seawall two feet higher after the flood year. In the decade since, no storm has topped it. The town's engineer refuses to call the wall a success, though: 'We have not been tested,' she says, 'by anything like the flood year.'

The engineer's refusal rests on the reasoning that
options: the wall is certainly too low
an untested defense has not yet demonstrated it can succeed
storms have become stronger every year
the town should not have rebuilt the wall
hints: What evidence would the engineer accept?
A storm comparable to the flood year has not occurred since.
Absence of failure without a real test is not proof of success.
expl: No storm like the flood year has tested the wall, so its success is undemonstrated rather than proven — the engineer's exact caution.

q:
The lecture hall's acoustics were designed for speech. _____ a string quartet that performed there last spring sounded strangely distant, as if playing from behind a curtain.

Which transition best completes the sentence?
hints: The second sentence pushes against the first's implication.
Designed well for speech — yet music sounded distant.
A result that runs against expectation takes a concessive transition.
expl: The distant sound contrasts with the hall's careful design, so the concessive 'Even so,' fits; result and addition transitions point the wrong way.

q:
In one district, students who practiced arithmetic facts for ten minutes daily gained, over a term, twice the fluency of a matched group that practiced for thirty minutes once a week. Total practice time was nearly equal; only its distribution differed.

Which conclusion is best supported by the study as described?
options: Longer weekly sessions are always superior.
With total time nearly equal, shorter daily practice accompanied greater fluency gains.
hints: Hold total time steady in your mind — it was nearly equal.
What differed was distribution: daily versus weekly.
The gain followed the daily distribution.
expl: Total time was nearly equal, so the difference tracks the distribution: short daily practice accompanied twice the fluency gain. Preference was never measured.

q:
(Transcript) Shopkeeper: 'The frames you ordered are ready — the oak ones, I mean. The walnut set is still at the finisher's and should be here by Friday.'

According to the shopkeeper, which frames are ready now?
hints: The speaker distinguishes the sets by their status.
Oak: ready. Walnut: still at the finisher's.
Only one set is described as ready.
expl: The oak frames are stated to be ready; the walnut set is still at the finisher's until Friday. Only the oak set is ready now.

q:
When the printing press reached a new town, its first products were rarely books. Printers earned their keep on the small and urgent: notices, forms, advertisements, and single-sheet announcements — work that had to be remade constantly and could not wait for a scribe.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Books were unpopular in new towns.
A press's early business was everyday job printing, not books, because that work was constant and urgent.
hints: Ask what filled the printer's order book and why.
Small, urgent, constantly remade work — notices and forms.
The reason given is constancy and urgency.
expl: The passage says printers lived on small urgent jobs that recurred constantly, while books were rare at first — choice B states both the fact and the reason.

q:
City crews planted rows of young maples along the avenue last spring. Within a year, summer temperatures on the shaded blocks measured several degrees cooler than on nearby unshaded streets, and shopkeepers reported that more pedestrians lingered outside their stores.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Planting trees is too expensive for most cities.
Newly planted street trees cooled the avenue and drew more foot traffic.
Maples grow faster than other street trees.
hints: Look for the choice that covers both effects mentioned.
The passage reports two results: cooler temperatures and more lingering pedestrians.
Reject choices that add claims the passage never makes.
expl: Both reported effects — cooling and increased foot traffic — appear in the passage. The other choices invent claims (cost, growth rate, shopkeeper preference) that the text never states.

q:
Bees communicate the location of flowers through a 'waggle dance' performed inside the hive. The angle of the dance relative to the sun tells watching bees the direction of the food source, while the dance's duration signals how far away it is.

According to the passage, the duration of the waggle dance communicates
hints: Match each detail to what the passage assigns to it.
Angle handles one thing; duration handles another.
The passage separates direction (angle) from distance (duration).
expl: The passage states plainly that duration signals distance, while angle signals direction. The other options are not assigned to duration anywhere in the text.

q:
A school garden club tracked its tomato plants for a month. Plants watered every other day grew taller than plants watered daily, which surprised the students, who had expected more water to mean more growth.

Which statement is best supported by the passage?
options: Tomatoes should never be watered daily.
In this club's month of tracking, less frequent watering coincided with taller plants.
hints: Stay inside what was actually observed: one club, one month.
Strong words like 'never' and 'kills' go beyond the evidence.
The supported claim is narrow: in this observation, the every-other-day plants grew taller.
expl: The passage reports one club's one-month observation. Only option B keeps that narrow scope; the others turn a single observation into universal rules the text never makes.

q:
When the factory switched to LED lighting, managers expected only lower electricity bills. Within months, however, supervisors also reported fewer errors on the night shift — a benefit nobody had predicted.

The author's purpose in the final clause — 'a benefit nobody had predicted' — is most likely to
options: emphasize that the second benefit was unexpected
hints: Ask why the author included this detail, not just what it says.
The sentence contrasts the expected benefit with the one that surprised everyone.
Purpose questions reward the function of the words in the passage.
expl: The clause underscores surprise: lower bills were expected, fewer errors were not. The author is emphasizing the unexpected bonus, not criticizing anyone or changing the subject.

q:
Despite the forecast of rain, the hikers set out early. By noon the sky had cleared, and the trail — muddy but passable — led them to the summit before the light faded.

As used in the passage, 'passable' most nearly means
hints: Use the surrounding action: the hikers used the trail and reached the summit.
Muddy 'but' passable — the word is contrasted with the mud, then they walked it.
Choose the meaning the sentence's own events prove.
expl: The hikers traveled the trail to the summit, so 'passable' must mean able to be traveled on — muddy, but usable. The context rules out the other meanings.

q:
In an experiment, two identical seedlings were placed in the same soil and light. One received plain water; the other received water mixed with a small amount of fertilizer. After three weeks, the fertilized seedling was noticeably taller.

Which question does this experiment best help answer?
options: Which soil is best for seedlings?
How much light do seedlings need?
hints: Find the one thing that differed between the two seedlings.
Soil and light were held the same; only the fertilizer changed.
An experiment answers questions about the variable it changes.
expl: Only one variable differed — fertilizer — so the experiment tests fertilizer's effect on growth. Soil, light, and water questions can't be answered because those were kept the same.

q:
A survey of 400 shoppers found that 62% choose a store mainly for its prices, 23% for its location, and 15% for its product selection.

Which conclusion is best supported by the survey?
options: Most shoppers rank product selection first.
Price is the most common main reason shoppers in this survey chose a store.
All shoppers care only about price.
hints: Let the largest percentage speak, and keep the claim inside the survey.
62% is a majority, and it belongs to prices.
Avoid absolutes ('never', 'all', 'only') the data doesn't support.
expl: With 62%, price is the most-cited main reason among these 400 shoppers. The other options contradict the data or stretch it into absolutes.

q:
(Transcript) Professor: 'Most students assume the desert tortoise survives the summer by finding shade. In fact, it survives by spending the hottest months underground, in burrows where the temperature stays far cooler than the surface.'

What does the professor mainly correct?
options: The idea that tortoises live in deserts
The assumption that shade is the tortoise's main survival strategy
The claim that burrows are cool
The belief that summers are hot
hints: Listen for the contrast: 'assume' versus 'in fact.'
The professor replaces one explanation with another.
Shade is the assumed strategy; burrows are the real one.
expl: The professor's 'in fact' corrects the assumption: shade is not the main strategy — underground burrows are. The other options are things the professor accepts, not corrects.

q:
(Transcript) Caller: 'I'd like to book the hall for Saturday the 14th — sorry, Saturday the 21st — for about fifty guests.'

According to the caller, the booking is for
hints: Speakers correct themselves; the final version is the answer.
The caller replaces the 14th with a new date.
Write down the corrected information, not the first version.
expl: The caller self-corrects from the 14th to the 21st. Listening tests plant these corrections constantly; the last stated version is the booking.

q:
Paragraph: 'Early attempts to build a flying machine failed for a simple reason: inventors copied the shape of birds without understanding the forces that keep a craft in the air. Only when researchers studied lift itself — measuring how air moves over a curved wing — did practical designs begin to appear.'

Which heading best fits the paragraph?
options: Early Setbacks Point Toward the Science of Lift
How to Build a Wing at Home
hints: A heading states the paragraph's whole gist, not one detail.
The paragraph moves from failed copying to studying lift.
Reject headings that are too broad, too narrow, or off-topic.
expl: The paragraph's arc is failure-through-copying followed by progress through understanding lift — exactly what heading B says. The others miss the arc or invent content.

q:
When the city replaced its diesel buses with electric ones, the transit director expected quieter streets. Within a year, however, mechanics reported something else: the electric buses needed far less brake work, because their motors slowed the vehicles by recovering energy instead of grinding pads.

The author's mention of brake work primarily serves to
options: argue that buses should be free
hints: Look for what the sentence adds beyond the expected point.
The director expected quieter streets; brake savings were not part of that expectation.
An added, unplanned advantage is an additional benefit.
expl: The passage sets up one expected gain (quieter streets) and then presents brake savings as a further, unexpected gain — an additional benefit, not a criticism or a mechanics lesson.

q:
A bakery that once sold only white and wheat loaves began offering rye, sourdough, and seeded varieties. Sales rose — but not, the owner admits, because customers suddenly preferred those breads. Most buyers still choose white; they simply visit more often now that the shop feels like a place where they might find something new.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Customers have stopped buying white bread.
A wider selection can raise sales by drawing customers in more often, even when their favorites stay the same.
Sourdough is the bakery's best-selling loaf.
Small bakeries cannot compete with large ones.
hints: Find the sentence that explains why sales rose.
The owner says favorites did not change; visits did.
The main idea must cover both the wider shelves and the unchanged favorites.
expl: Sales rose because variety brought customers through the door more often, while their actual favorite — white bread — stayed the same. Only choice B captures both halves of that point.

q:
To the relief of the night staff, the hospital's new scheduling software proved tractable: within a week, even the least technical nurses were building their own rotas without help.

As used in the passage, 'tractable' most nearly means
hints: The staff mastered the software within a week.
A thing people can handle easily is manageable.
Match the word to the outcome described: quick, unaided use.
expl: The nurses used the software on their own within a week, so 'tractable' here means easy to manage. The other choices contradict or ignore that outcome.

q:
The museum extended its hours on Fridays. _____ attendance on Friday evenings doubled within two months.

Which transition best completes the sentence?
hints: Name the relationship between the two facts.
Longer hours came first; higher attendance followed from them.
A following effect is signalled by a result transition.
expl: The doubled attendance is the effect of the extended hours, so the result transition 'As a result,' is the logical fit.

q:
Neither the coach nor the players _____ aware of the schedule change until the morning of the game.

Which verb form correctly completes the sentence?
hints: With 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.
The nearer subject here is 'players', which is plural.
The sentence is set in the past ('until the morning of the game'), so choose the plural past form.
expl: With neither/nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'players' (plural), and the past-tense setting ('until the morning of the game') requires 'were'.

q:
In a trial of two compost mixtures, researchers kept soil, water, and sunlight identical for forty tomato plants. The twenty plants fed mixture B produced, on average, 18 percent more fruit by weight than the twenty fed mixture A.

The results of the trial best support which conclusion?
options: Mixture B caused the higher yield under the trial's conditions.
Mixture A is poisonous to plants.
hints: Every condition except the mixture was held the same.
When only one variable differs, a difference in outcome points to that variable.
The claim must stay inside the trial's conditions.
expl: Because soil, water, and sunlight were identical, the yield difference is attributable to the mixtures — and the supported claim stays within those trial conditions.

q:
(Transcript) Manager: 'Before we approve the budget, note that the figures on page two are last year's. The updated totals are in the appendix, and they are slightly higher.'

According to the manager, where are the current budget figures?
hints: The manager corrects an assumption about page two.
Page two holds last year's figures.
The updated totals are named directly: the appendix.
expl: The manager says page two is out of date and the updated totals are in the appendix — a direct statement, not an inference.

q:
Paragraph: 'Before the telegraph, news of a battle might take weeks to cross an ocean, and by the time it arrived it was history. The telegraph collapsed that distance to minutes, and newspapers began competing not on what had happened but on how quickly they could say it.'

Which heading best fits the paragraph?
options: Famous Battles of the Nineteenth Century
How the Telegraph Changed the Speed of News
hints: A heading must cover the whole arc: before, then after.
The paragraph is about speed, not battles or instructions.
The telegraph's effect on news timing is the through-line.
expl: The paragraph contrasts slow news before the telegraph with minutes-fast news after it — a change in the speed of news. The other headings are too narrow or off-topic.

q:
Farmers in the valley had long planted a single variety of potato. When a blight arrived in 2019, fields planted with that variety failed almost completely, while the few farms that had kept three or four varieties lost only the susceptible rows.

It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that
options: planting several varieties reduced the farms' total losses
the valley now grows no potatoes
hints: Compare the outcomes of the two planting strategies.
Single-variety fields failed almost completely; varied farms lost only some rows.
An inference must stay close to that comparison.
expl: The varied farms lost only the susceptible rows while single-variety fields failed almost completely, so variety reduced total losses. The passage does not support the stronger or unrelated claims.

q:
The trail guide warns that the last mile of the canyon path is exposed, with no shade and no water. Hikers _____ begin that stretch before noon in summer.

Which choice best completes the sentence with the meaning the guide intends?
hints: Connect the warning to the advice it implies.
No shade and no water at midday is a hazard.
The intended meaning is caution about timing.
expl: A warning about heat exposure implies hikers should not start the exposed stretch at midday; choice A carries that caution.

q:
A library system noticed that books displayed face-out on the ends of shelves were borrowed three times as often as the same books shelved spine-out. The librarians changed nothing else — not the collection, not the hours — only the orientation of a few hundred covers.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Face-out displays increased borrowing of the same books.
Borrowing has declined in recent years.
hints: Only one thing changed; one result followed.
Same books, same hours — only orientation differed.
The main idea links that single change to the borrowing result.
expl: With everything else held constant, rotating covers face-out tripled borrowing of the identical books. That change-and-result pair is the main idea.

q: Which option is correct?
options: The committee released its findings on Friday, it recommended three changes to the admissions process.
The committee released its findings on Friday; it recommended three changes to the admissions process.
The committee released its findings on Friday recommended three changes to the admissions process.
The committee released its findings on Friday. Recommended three changes to the admissions process.
hints: The sentence joins two complete thoughts.
A comma alone cannot join them — that is a comma splice.
A semicolon joins two complete, related thoughts correctly.
expl: The original joins two independent clauses with only a comma. The semicolon version joins them correctly; the others keep the splice, drop punctuation, or create a fragment.

q:
Beekeepers in the region lost a third of their hives in a single winter. Surveys found no single cause: a parasite weakened the colonies, a late frost caught them short of stores, and a wet autumn had kept bees from foraging on the last warm days.

According to the passage, the hive losses resulted from
hints: The passage explicitly rejects a single cause.
Count the stresses it lists: parasite, frost, wet autumn.
Together, not alone, is the passage's answer.
expl: The passage names three stresses — parasite, late frost, and a wet autumn — and says there was no single cause, so the losses came from several stresses together.

q:
When the factory moved its start time from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m., supervisors braced for complaints from the early crew. _____, the early crew asked to keep the new time: the extra hour of sleep, several said, was worth more than the earlier finish.

Which transition best completes the sentence?
hints: What was expected, and what actually happened?
Complaints were expected; approval happened instead.
An outcome opposite to expectation takes a contrast transition.
expl: The crew's approval contradicts the expected complaints, so the contrast transition 'In contrast,' fits the turn.

q:
The old bridge was, by every engineering measure, obsolete — too narrow for modern traffic, costly to maintain, and due for replacement. Yet when demolition was proposed, the town council chamber filled with residents who had crossed it on foot every day of their lives and could not imagine the river without it.

The author includes the residents' reaction most likely to
options: prove the bridge was well engineered
show that a structure's value is not measured only in engineering terms
argue that councils should never replace bridges
explain how demolition is carried out
hints: Weigh the two halves of the passage against each other.
The first half measures the bridge by engineering; the second measures it by daily life.
The reaction introduces a different kind of value.
expl: The passage contrasts engineering measures with the bridge's place in residents' daily lives, showing value beyond engineering terms — without claiming demolition is never right.

q:
A survey of 900 commuters found that 48 percent would accept a longer commute for a quieter train car, 31 percent for a guaranteed seat, and 21 percent for faster Wi-Fi.

Which conclusion is best supported by the survey?
options: Quiet was the most common first priority among the options offered.
Commutes are getting longer every year.
hints: Compare the three percentages directly.
48 percent is larger than 31 and 21.
The largest share named quiet — first among the offered options.
expl: Quiet drew 48 percent, the largest share of the three options, so it was the most common priority among those offered. The passage says nothing about trends over time.

q:
(Transcript) Librarian: 'The reading room closes at eight tonight, not nine — we're hosting the school awards in there from seven thirty, so please gather your things by seven fifteen.'

According to the librarian, by what time should readers gather their things?
hints: Several times are mentioned; find the one attached to gathering things.
Eight is closing; seven thirty is the awards start.
The instruction says 'by seven fifteen'.
expl: The librarian gives three times, but the gathering instruction is explicit: 'by seven fifteen.' The other options attach to closing and the event start.

q:
Paragraph: 'Coral reefs occupy a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. The reef's structure — built by colonies of small animals over centuries — creates the crevices, shade, and currents that so many other species depend on.'

Which heading best fits the paragraph?
options: The Largest Animals in the Ocean
Small Area, Immense Shelter: Why Reefs Hold So Much Life
How to Build an Artificial Reef
hints: The heading must match both the small size and the large effect.
The paragraph explains why so much life gathers there: structure.
Only one heading carries the size-versus-life contrast.
expl: The paragraph's point is the contrast between the reefs' tiny area and the quarter of marine species they shelter, explained by their structure — exactly what heading B states.

q:
Unlike her colleagues, who announced each result the moment it appeared, Dr. Osei was reticent about her experiment, saying only that 'the work is not finished' until the final trial had been replicated twice.

As used in the passage, 'reticent' most nearly means
hints: Contrast her behavior with her colleagues'.
They announced at once; she said almost nothing until the end.
Speaking little, by choice, is reluctance to speak.
expl: Dr. Osei withheld comment until replication was complete, in contrast to colleagues who announced immediately — 'reticent' means reluctant to speak.
